en: Saying that this was how matters stood,
Quickly uttering his prayer,
He rode out to meet the envoy,
To travel among the people,
Then Jeljetpes,
Casting off all his sorrow,
His wrath turned bloody,
His brow struck against another.
“I will level and take his land,”
The boar in the midst of the land,
“I will strike the rival Kyrgyz.”
Sending word through his rival,
Giving news to the white-kalpak people,
His men bound their hands,
Driving the people along the dusty road,
Gathering the people who obeyed his word,
This hellish infidel’s,
Striking against mountain and stone,
Gathering the neighbors into an army,
Leading the road among his equals,
One of his soldiers was sent upon the road.
Tearing apart sinew and strength,
The descendants of the Kyrgyz heroes,
Rejoicing when the heroes migrated,
“I will seize one from among the heroes.”
If the grunting boar starts a quarrel,
I will send him down a separate road,
I pray for the people’s safety,
For his people on the distant side,
If there are people, I will ask,
I wish for the people’s harvest,
Let this safety not be lost,
Restrain your wrath before Tengir,
Cast down the multitude’s fire,
Shielding his treasure and host.
There was one who could bring upheaval,
All four of his sides were fully equipped.
He had livestock beyond tens of thousands,
The Kyrgyz strength endured through the ages,
He had power for the gravest deeds,
Let him not surrender it to his lesser rival,
The people broke the command of the realm,
When angered, his venom was fierce,
This Chyngteñir, like a whole nation,
Was a merciless hero,
His age cut sharply across the times,
The signs of the many worlds,
A single girl will make everything constrained,
She will cover the moonlit world like snow.
This incorrigible monster,
Let him not give her to his lesser rival.
Though they plead, no blood will remain,
This brute is strong as a boar,
Though they supplicate, nothing will remain,
He will destroy what is called a people,
This will strike women and young children,
These enraged Kyrgyz,
This blood-guilt makes even the noble reflect.
Last night he spoke these words,
I nearly fell among the old men,
I escaped from the harsh command,
My crest and my mottled raiment,
From the core of my heart,
I nearly remained upon the ridge,
Slipping upon the road,
I nearly remained at the horde.
When the infidel was born,
The sun burned scorching hot,
They witnessed the searing calamity,
Ninety brides and ninety girls,
From the women of the district and village,
Their hearts burst from fright.
A soul sheltered from his wrath,
The towering hero,
Who could halt what moved in the mountains,
When ten came through the ravine,
He cursed all the khans.
When ten thousand came,
He swept away all the worthy men,
He burned them like a threshing floor,
He made the stone steed a lord,
He forgot the one mounted on stone,
He made strife upon the barren ridge.
He reeled as though struck,
Toward Beijing where strife was woven,
He became a powerful, hard-fighting man,
Destroying the warriors,
He laid low those who faced him,
With three others he became khan,
One day Jeljetpes became the man in command.
The waters of this mountain did not surge within,
Toward Beijing where strife was woven,
Hewn with an axe,
Like a cauldron forty fathoms wide,
When broken, it opened by itself,
Saying he would not leave Beijing in peace,
Saying no enemy would advance upon it,
The solitary man who made preparations,
The man who stood barring the way,
Saying he would not cast his eye upon us,
When the hidden one vanished,
Saying he would not march at a villain’s cry,
This glittering Beijing,
House after house was emptied,
They began carrying stones like mountains,
They set boys to the task,
The people reached Kakan,
If he seized the people in former times,
When livestock flourished in spring,
“Hurry,” yet he did not hurry.
He comes on without taking heed,
He lets neither game nor beast advance,
Not letting the free rider advance,
He sends the difficult yellow host wandering,
He chilled the people and slaughtered them,
Bound to one wrathful man,
God has surely struck this people.
This cry of Ysyman,
In this rage, grim Tengir will not draw near,
Unable to escape this wrath,
This khagan’s affairs will not be set right,
What he said again,
His land diminishes by the day,
Chyng Tengir stands orphaned,
What this Kalmak has inflicted,
Driving them in clamor by the horns like sheep,
Chyng Tengir keeps slaughtering them,
As for these Chinese, through the age,
Chyng Tengir was about to go,
These many afflictions upon the world,
Chyng Tengir was about to impose.
At the old khan’s command,
When he ascended the new throne,
The pacer whom even the wind could not catch,
Saying, “You seized and rode it without permission,”
What kind of conduct was that from you?
Saying, “You put it on without permission,”
His menace mounting from beneath,
Before sixty hulking champions,
Making Kolkormon press him down,
His terrible presence deafening the ears,
Before six hulking champions,
Doing a deed beyond human measure,
Upon the solid flesh of his fat rump,
He had six hundred lashes struck.
You survived instead of dying,
Crying “oi-boi,” drenched and bleeding,
His wretched soul shrieking,
Your bones, let alone your flesh,
Then one burned with grief arose from the Kyrgyz.
The wily fox was in his fold,
The marked fox was slaughtered,
He placed the moon-mark upon his people,
His whole body was shattered,
His heart would not remain still,
From this deed Jeljetti
Could not bring matters to completion.
Thus he tormented them,
Twisting as he faced forward,
The one-eyed Maady hero,
Wearing the coat of the gray falcon,
Mounted after receiving news from Torum,
He had an eye like a half-formed hand.
He possessed the nature he was born with,
“I will wound him,” he came.
Setting twins against their equal,
He would block that enemy,
At the place from which none returns.
In the form of a fierce fox,
Into the enemy’s hellish pit,
He cast him and destroyed him.
He spread out the grave affair,
His single eye was opened,
With wrath like lightning,
The people and realm saw it, they said,
Like a black monster among the wealthy,
The appointed hour had come, they said,
Opening the sieve and spoiling the work,
He stood from idleness, they said,
He began wrath against a thousand.
From among those wise in counsel,
From those skilled in speech and eloquence,
The people he reproached stirred,
At the head of the people stood a captain of ten,
From a lone bearer of wise news,
He displayed his wondrous strength,
He began his forceful wrath.
Because of the one-eyed archer,
He subdued the people of Kakan,
Here he shed their blood.
Many bellies were left empty,
Only this remnant of my land remained.
Because of this woman’s venom,
What was it like? The khan wept,
All populous Beijing wept.
Even the thundering sun cannot reach it,
If I crush it, words will not prevail,
The eye cannot grasp such overwhelming force.
Thus spoke Jeljetpes,
Telling this to those who would go,
Firmly instructing the envoys,
Jeljetpes went out to his people.
Finishing the people’s business,
Jeljetpes set out to depart,
What remedy is there for this strange affair?
Jeljetpes went out after his elder,
Toward his Kyrgyz people,
Jeljetpes set out to find them,
Having seen humiliation and hardship,
Jeljetpes said he would see it,
Driving the herds this way,
Jeljetpes said he would see it.
Hear of all the champions,
The khan’s wrath will be unleashed,
Seeing the place of death,
The gray day drove the mount onward.
Mounted on a lean yellow horse,
The poor hero, unable to reach him,
Cried in anguish and rode hard,
The wrathful khagan who roamed,
Leading those who obeyed,
The corrupt eye saw it,
Let us sink into the earth.
Having gone and returned,
“Let us enter elsewhere.”
Thus spoke Jeljetpes,
Making it known to the heroes,
Bringing the boys to obey his words,
Providing sustenance for his people’s hearts,
Jeljetpes intended to ensnare them.
From Chyngteñir’s net,
From the hand of the wrathful day,
Jeljetpes was about to remain.
Before the sign of the sun arose,
Such a stern and imposing hero,
The accomplished champion Jeljetpes,
“If we leave together, you have seen it,” he said,
There was no movement and no quarrel,
“Simply take warning from me,” he said,
I came with the horse lathered and spent,
Jeljetpes prevailed over all of you,
“I will recover your due,” he said,
Without sitting and without ceasing to move,
“Remain where you understand,” he said,
Khan Bangyr said this,
He told of the dreadful hardship he had seen,
After the man departed again,
Jeljetpes entered upon the road.
The one he led was a heroic champion,
His breast was full of deep sorrow,
Toward the churned dust,
The ill-starred wanderer was to come.
Chyngteñir, who traveled with thousands,
From the snare laid over these people,
Had saved a man without entanglement.
Thus spoke Jeljetpes,
